content: Recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) is known to enhance protein synthesis. It is utilized in patients with burns covering more than 40% of the total body surface area (TBSA), as these individuals often experience increased protein breakdown and reduced protein synthesis. This disruption in protein metabolism is associated with delayed wound healing in both burn wounds and donor sites. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of rhGH on the healing rates of burn wounds and donor sites in individuals with burns. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, DARE, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL, up to September 2014. The study focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared rhGH with other interventions, such as oxandrolone or placebo, in both adult and pediatric burn patients. The selection criteria included RCTs that assessed the primary outcomes of burn wound and donor site healing, as well as the occurrence of wound infections. Secondary outcomes included mortality rates, hospital stay duration, scar assessment, and adverse events such as hyperglycemia and septicemia. Two independent reviewers evaluated the quality of the trials and extracted the relevant data. A total of 13 RCTs involving 701 participants were included in the analysis. Six of these trials involved children aged 1 to 18 years, while seven focused on adults aged 18 to 65 years. The mean TBSA affected in the participants was greater than 49%. Twelve studies compared rhGH with placebo, and one study compared rhGH with oxandrolone. In adults, rhGH treatment significantly accelerated burn wound healing compared to placebo, reducing healing time by an average of 9.07 days (95% confidence interval [CI]: 4.39 to 13.76). Donor site healing time was also significantly shorter in adults treated with rhGH, with a reduction of 3.15 days (95% CI: 1.54 to 4.75). In children, pooled data from two studies showed that rhGH reduced donor site healing time by 1.70 days (95% CI: 0.87 to 2.53). No studies were identified that reported on the outcome of wound infections. However, the incidence of hyperglycemia was notably higher in adults receiving rhGH compared to placebo, with a risk ratio (RR) of 2.43 (95% CI: 1.54 to 3.85). This increased risk of hyperglycemia was not observed in children. When data from both adults and children were combined, rhGH treatment was associated with a significantly higher risk of hyperglycemia (RR: 2.65; 95% CI: 1.68 to 4.16). In conclusion, there is evidence suggesting that rhGH may promote faster healing of burn wounds and donor sites in both adults and children with burns affecting more than 40% of TBSA. Additionally, rhGH treatment may reduce the length of hospital stay without increasing mortality or scarring. However, the use of rhGH is associated with an elevated risk of hyperglycemia, particularly in adults. It is important to note that these findings are based on studies with small sample sizes and potential biases, underscoring the need for larger, high-quality trials to confirm these results.
